page_title: Why you should probably be using SQLite

sources.entry: Why you should probably be using SQLite | Epic Web Dev

summary.title: Why you should probably be using SQLite
summary.one_liner: SQLite can simplify most web apps by removing a database service, cutting latency, and easing development and testing, though it has real limits around subscriptions, external access, and enums.
takeaways: SQLite runs embedded as a single file, so there is no separate database service to run, pay for, or babysit.
Co-locating SQLite with the app removes app-to-database network latency, which reduces the impact of the n+1 query problem.
Multi-instance setups need extra tooling such as LiteFS (replication) or Turso (embedded replicas).
Development and testing are easier because each test or app instance can have its own database file with no port or server conflicts.
Weaknesses include no subscriptions, no direct external client connections, no TimescaleDB-style plugins, and no enums.
summary.summary: The author argues that for most web applications SQLite is a better default than MySQL or Postgres, because the whole database is a single file. He covers zero-latency local access, fewer services to run, replication options (LiteFS, Turso embedded replicas), the very large size limits, and simpler local development and per-test databases. He closes with a candid list of weaknesses: no subscriptions, no direct external connections, no TimescaleDB-like plugins, and no enums. The piece is an opinion essay with experience from his own apps rather than a hands-on tutorial.
